faqs.a: backdrop-filter applies graphical effects — blur, brightness, contrast, saturate — to the area behind an element, while filter applies them to the element itself. Glassmorphism needs backdrop-filter because the frosted look comes from blurring whatever is behind the card, not the card's own content.
faqs.q: What is the difference between backdrop-filter and filter?

faqs.a: Add both lines: backdrop-filter: blur(12px); and -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(12px);. Safari required the prefixed version for years, and older iOS versions still do. This tool's output includes the prefix automatically.
faqs.q: Why does my glass effect not work in Safari?

faqs.a: Three things sell the illusion: a semi-transparent background (10–25% opacity), a 1px light border at slightly higher opacity than the fill, and a soft drop shadow. Also make sure something colorful sits behind the card — glass over a flat gray background just looks gray.
faqs.q: How do I make glassmorphism look good, not washed out?

faqs.a: Text directly on glass can fail contrast checks, especially over busy backgrounds. Use dark text on light glass or white text on dark glass, keep the blur strong enough to mute the background, and test with a contrast checker. Never put critical small text on very transparent glass.

backdrop-filter is GPU-accelerated but still costs performance: each glass element forces the browser to re-render the backdrop. A few cards are fine; dozens of large blurred panels — especially animating — can drop frames on phones. Use it sparingly on mobile layouts.
